title: Thieves Swap Premium GPUs for Budget Cards in Chinese Esports Hotels, Foiled by Power Outage
excerpt: A group replaced RTX 5080 graphics cards with RTX 3060s across multiple gaming PCs in an esports hotel, only to be caught when a blackout forced staff to reboot the machines.
body:
• Thieves checked into a Chinese esports hotel and swapped high-end RTX 5080 GPUs with older RTX 3060 cards across multiple gaming PCs, a scheme worth roughly $12,000.
  • The heist was discovered only when a power outage forced hotel staff to restart machines, revealing the mismatched hardware.
  • The incident is the latest in a growing wave of GPU-related crime in China's booming esports hotel industry, where high-end components sit unguarded in guest rooms.

GPU thieves in China have leveled up. Rather than simply ripping expensive graphics cards out of gaming PCs — an approach that gets noticed the moment the next guest boots up — a group of hotel guests took a subtler route: they swapped premium Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 cards for budget RTX 3060s across multiple machines, pocketing hardware worth roughly $12,000 in the process.

The scheme worked because the PCs still functioned after the swap. A lower-tier GPU can run the same operating system and basic software without throwing any obvious red flags to hotel staff. The thieves might have gotten away with it entirely had an unplanned power outage not forced employees to reboot every machine in the facility, according to reports. When the systems came back online, staff noticed performance discrepancies and checked the hardware — discovering that the high-end RTX 5080 cards had been replaced with RTX 3060s worth a fraction of the price.

A Booming Industry's Blind Spot

Esports hotels are a massive business in China, with over 20,000 such establishments operating across the country as of 2023, according to industry estimates reported by BlazeT rends. The hotels offer rooms equipped with high-spec gaming PCs — often featuring the latest Nvidia and AMD processors — marketed to gamers who want premium hardware for extended sessions.

https://x.com/PCMag/status/2089462793455997170

That business model creates an obvious security problem: thousands of dollars in easily removable components sitting in private rooms with screwdriver access and no surveillance on the hardware itself.

This latest incident follows a pattern. In a widely reported case last year, guests at another Chinese esports hotel stripped Ryzen 7 9800X3D processors and RTX 5070 graphics cards from multiple PCs before checking out, according to PC Gamer. The hotel owner discovered the theft only after the guests blocked him on WeChat. The stolen components were valued at $5,000 to $10,000.

"The 9800X3D and 5070… OMG. Even Logitech GPW was stolen. But they didn't take the RAM sticks… maybe they didn't know how to remove them?"

— Esports hotel owner, via Reddit

More recently, two men identified as Li and Cheng were arrested after a string of RAM thefts from esports hotels in Shihezi City, Xinjiang province. The pair pried 16 memory sticks from hotel PCs over two weeks, selling them for roughly $1,950 on secondhand markets, according to Chinese state media via Tom's Hardware.

Why GPUs Are the New Gold

The GPU swap scheme reflects a broader reality: graphics cards have become extraordinarily valuable, driven by demand from both gamers and the AI industry. The RTX 5080, with a manufacturer's suggested retail price of $999, now commands prices closer to $1,250 on the open market due to persistent supply shortages and overwhelming demand from AI developers. The RTX 5090, priced at $1,999 MSRP, frequently sells for 65% to 75% above that.

In South Korea, a thief broke into a computer hardware store earlier this year and made off with RTX 5080 and RTX 5090 cards worth approximately $15,000. The suspect was caught within a day, according to Korean media outlet Newsis.

The swap approach is more sophisticated than outright theft. By leaving a functioning — if inferior — GPU in place, the thieves buy themselves time before discovery. In this case, only an unforeseeable event exposed the scheme.

What's Next

Chinese esports hotel operators are increasingly looking at hardware security measures, including physical cages around gaming rigs and software-based component monitoring that can flag hardware changes in real time. WeChat-linked guest registration, standard in Chinese hotels, gives operators a direct identity trail, making it difficult for thieves to remain anonymous — though that has not prevented the wave of incidents.

For the broader PC hardware market, the trend underscores a simple point: as GPUs become more valuable, the incentive to steal them grows in proportion. The swap method may be new, but the underlying economics are not going away anytime soon.
